explanations.answer: Rub them in their hands and eat them
explanations.explanation: That's what Luke 6:1 says: the disciples "began to pick the heads of grain, rub them in their hands, and eat them." No oven, no timer, no cooling rack. Just hands and a hungry walk through a field. I've baked a lot of batches, and even I have never made a snack that fast.

explanations.answer: Gather them into baskets to sell
explanations.explanation: Baskets and selling never show up in this verse. Luke 6:1 says the disciples rub the grain in their hands and eat it. Nobody is running a grain stand here. I think the only business going on is lunch.

explanations.answer: Carry them to the priests as an offering
explanations.explanation: Close to a church-sounding answer, but the text doesn't go there. Luke 6:1 says the disciples "rub them in their hands, and eat them." The grain goes straight from their hands to their mouths. Nobody walks it to a priest.

explanations.answer: Why they're doing what's unlawful on the Sabbath
explanations.explanation: Right on the money. The Pharisees ask, "Why are you doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath?" (Luke 6:2). Their question is about the day. Not the field, not the grain, just what's happening on the Sabbath.

explanations.answer: Why they're picking grain in another man's field
explanations.explanation: The Pharisees never bring up whose field it is. Their question in Luke 6:2 is, "Why are you doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath?" The whole complaint hangs on the day. The field never comes up.

explanations.answer: Why they're eating without washing their hands
explanations.explanation: Hand washing isn't in this passage at all. The Pharisees ask, "Why are you doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath?" (Luke 6:2). The word that matters in their question is Sabbath. Nobody here says a thing about soap.

True, and it's right there in Luke 6:4: David "entered the house of God." David, Israel's king, did this when he and his companions were hungry. Jesus points back to that moment when the Pharisees question Him. I'd say Jesus really did bring the receipts.

This one's actually true. Luke 6:4 says David "entered the house of God." David, Israel's king, did this when he and his companions were hungry. Jesus brings it up to answer the Pharisees. No stress, baker, now you've got it for next time.

Bread it is. Luke 6:4 says David "took the consecrated bread and gave it to his companions." He didn't keep it all to himself, he shared it. Consecrated means set apart, so this wasn't ordinary bread off the counter.

Oil sounds holy enough, but it's not in Luke 6:4. The verse says David "took the consecrated bread and gave it to his companions." Hungry men need something to eat, and that's what he took. Bread, baker, not oil.
Wine isn't in this verse. Luke 6:4 says David "took the consecrated bread and gave it to his companions." He and his companions were hungry, and the text names bread. That's the word to hold onto.
Yes. Luke 6:4 says David "ate what is lawful only for the priests to eat." That's what makes Jesus' example so striking. The bread was set apart for the priests, and David ate it anyway.

Interesting guess, since David became king, but that's not what the verse says. Luke 6:4 says the bread is "lawful only for the priests to eat." That's why Jesus' example stands out. David ate what was set apart for the priests.

Elders aren't mentioned in this verse. Luke 6:4 says David "ate what is lawful only for the priests to eat." The priests are the ones the bread was set apart for. Easy one to mix up when you're thinking about leaders.
That's the declaration. Jesus says, "The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath" (Luke 6:5). Lord means He has authority over the day. After a debate about what's lawful, that's a big thing to say.
Keeper sounds close, and I can see why you picked it. But Jesus says, "The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath" (Luke 6:5). One word makes the difference. Lord, not keeper.
Servant isn't the word Jesus uses. He says, "The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath" (Luke 6:5). Lord is the one who has authority over the day. Keep that word in your pocket, baker.

explanations.answer: If He will heal on the Sabbath
explanations.explanation: That's what Luke 6:7 says. The scribes and Pharisees were "watching Him closely to see if He would heal on the Sabbath." They were looking for a reason to accuse Him. I think that's the longest stare in the whole synagogue.

explanations.answer: If He will read from the scroll
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say anything about a scroll. Luke 6:7 says they were watching to see "if He would heal on the Sabbath." They were looking for a reason to accuse Jesus. Reading wasn't what they were waiting for.

explanations.answer: If He will leave the synagogue early
explanations.explanation: Leaving early isn't in this verse. Luke 6:7 says the scribes and Pharisees were watching "to see if He would heal on the Sabbath." Jesus was in the synagogue teaching (Luke 6:6). The thing they were watching for was a healing.

explanations.answer: Get up and stand among us
explanations.explanation: Right. Luke 6:8 says Jesus told the man, "Get up and stand among us." And the man "got up and stood there." Jesus does this knowing their thoughts, with everyone watching. I think the man needed some courage right then.
That's not what Jesus says. In Luke 6:8 He tells the man, "Get up and stand among us." The man gets up and stands there, right in the middle of the room. Nothing about outside.
Jesus doesn't send him away. Luke 6:8 says He told the man, "Get up and stand among us," and the man "got up and stood there." Right then, in front of everyone. No other day needed.

Evil is the first blank. Jesus asks, "which is lawful on the Sabbath: to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy it?" (Luke 6:9). Good and evil are set side by side. He asks the question right in front of them.
Destroy is the second blank. Jesus says, "to save life or to destroy it?" (Luke 6:9). Save life on one side, destroy on the other. It's a question that leaves no room to hide.
Nothing doesn't fit here. Jesus asks, "to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy it?" (Luke 6:9). The two choices He gives are good or evil. Doing nothing isn't one of them.
Ignore is a sneaky one, but it's not in the verse. Jesus asks, "to save life or to destroy it?" (Luke 6:9). The word He uses is destroy. Save and destroy are the two sides.

Rest feels natural on a Sabbath, I'll give you that. But Jesus asks, "to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy it?" (Luke 6:9). Evil and destroy are the words in the blanks. Rest isn't part of His question.

That's it. After looking around at all of them, Jesus says to the man, "Stretch out your hand" (Luke 6:10). A withered hand, and a command to stretch it out. That's a lot to ask, and I think it took some faith.
No washing here. Luke 6:10 says Jesus told the man, "Stretch out your hand." That's the whole instruction. Short and simple.

explanations.answer: Show your hand to the priest
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't send him to a priest in this passage. In Luke 6:10 He says, "Stretch out your hand." The man is right there in the synagogue. The healing happens on the spot.
Not quite, baker. Luke 6:10 says the man "did so, and it was restored." He stretched out his hand when Jesus told him to. No refusing in the text.
False is right. Jesus says, "Stretch out your hand," and Luke 6:10 says, "He did so, and it was restored." The man doesn't refuse. He does it, and his hand is made whole.
Rage is the word. Luke 6:11 says the scribes and Pharisees "were filled with rage." A man's hand was just restored, and this is how they react. I think this part is heavy.
That would be a nice ending, but the text says something else. Luke 6:11 says the scribes and Pharisees "were filled with rage." A man's hand had just been restored. I think this part is heavy.
Wonder would've been a different story. But Luke 6:11 says the scribes and Pharisees "were filled with rage." That's the word the text uses. I think this part is heavy.
True. Luke 6:11 says the scribes and Pharisees "began to discuss with one another what they might do to Jesus." They talk it over together. I think this is a heavy moment, and the story isn't over.

This one is true, baker. Luke 6:11 says the scribes and Pharisees "began to discuss with one another what they might do to Jesus." They talk it over together. I think this is a heavy moment, and the story isn't over.
